articles.title: Rajnath launches India’s first fleet support ship ‘Surya’ at Visakhapatnam; witnesses delivery of 2,000th aero-engine in Koraput
articles.summary: In a big boost for India’s maritime capabilities, defence minister Rajnath Singh on Tuesday launched ‘Surya’, the country’s first indigenously-built fleet
articles.body: In a big boost for India’s maritime capabilities, defence minister Rajnath Singh on Tuesday launched ‘Surya’, the country’s first indigenously-built fleet support ship (FSS-1), laid the keel for the fifth ship in the series (FSS-5), and inaugurated the upgraded Slipway-4 and 300-tonne Goliath crane at Hindustan Shipyard Limited (HSL) in Visakhapatnam.Thereafter, he went to Odisha’s Koraput to witness the delivery of the 2,000th aero-engine by Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL).Fleet support ships will act as floating logistics hubs that will keep Indian Navy's warships and carrier battle groups operational at sea for extended periods by providing fuel, fresh water, ammunition and dry provisions to frontline ships and even act as on-board maintenance workshops.Describing the “three milestones” as symbols of India’s growing maritime capability, Rajnath said, “The launch of FSS1 is a symbol of achievement, keel laying of FSS-5 is a symbol of resolve and the new Slipway is a symbol of our growing capability,” he said,Rajnath said the vessels would enhance Indian Navy’s reach, endurance and operational effectiveness in the Indian Ocean region. “Fleet support ships provide this critical capability by enabling at-sea replenishment and supporting naval operations over prolonged periods, thereby enhancing the fleet’s operational endurance,” he said.The defence minister had recently announced that a record 18 warships would be commissioned or inducted in 2026, marking the largest single-year force expansion in its history. Currently, around 45 active warship construction projects are under way, with orders for additional vessels and submarines approved or in the pipeline. With the Rajnath-led defence ministry pushing for self-reliance in naval shipbuilding, more than 75% of the content on these newly-built warships is now made in India.The upgraded Slipway-4 has been extended and strengthened to enable HSL to build and launch ships of up to 45,000 DWT. The 300-tonne Goliath Crane spanning Slipways 3 and 4 has been designed and manufactured by L&T Geostructure with Konecranes under Make in India. The new infrastructure will strengthen HSL’s ability to undertake larger and more complex shipbuilding programmes and support modern block construction.“Self-reliance is an important milestone, but global competitiveness is the next big leap,” Rajnath said while stressing that Indian shipyards should be able to compete on quality, cost, technology, delivery and reliability with the world’s leading shipyards.Calling for Visakhapatnam to be developed as a maritime industrial hub, Rajnath said the presence of Eastern Naval Command, Naval Dockyard, HSL, and Visakhapatnam Port provides the city with the “foundation for an integrated maritime ecosystem”.Recalling the launch of the first ship built in independent India ‘Jala Usha’ at Visakhapatnam in 1948, the minister highlighted India’s long-standing maritime heritage, noting that the country’s relationship with the sea dates back to ancient times.He described HSL as a custodian of India’s national maritime capability and lauded its contribution to the country’s maritime and defence requirements for more than eight decades. He highlighted HSL’s attainment of Miniratna Category-I status in 2025 after it came under the defence ministry as an important milestone reflecting its transformation and sustained efforts.“Our goal should be simple and clear — Design better, build faster, deliver on time. Operate efficiently and do maintenance effectively,” Rajnath said.At Koraput, Rajnath announced the establishment of a second production line for Shakti engines. Describing the milestone delivery of 2,000th aero-engine by HAL as a significant achievement in India’s aerospace journey, he called for strengthening indigenous capabilities in the design, development, testing, manufacturing and maintenance of advanced aero-engines, stressing that mastery of propulsion technology is essential for self-reliance in the aerospace and defence sector.“Today is a historic day for HAL Koraput. The division has today delivered its 2000th engine. This is more than a production milestone. It is a symbol of six decades of engineering capability, skilled manpower and commitment to strengthening India’s defence preparedness. I am extremely pleased to be part of this remarkable journey. HAL Koraput has also crossed another significant milestone. It has overhauled more than 9,000 engines. Behind these numbers is the skill and dedication of the engineers and technicians who keep India’s critical platforms mission-ready,” Rajnath later posted on X.He highlighted HAL Koraput’s contribution to military aviation, noting that its engines have powered frontline aircraft, including MiG-21, MiG-27, MiG-29 and Su-30MKI. He stated that while production provides new capability, overhaul extends service life, making both critical for military preparedness. The production of AL-31FP engines for the Su-30MKI is an important step in strengthening India’s indigenous engine manufacturing capability.The minister further said on X, “Despite global supply-chain disruptions and raw-material challenges, the Koraput team delivered its first engine ahead of schedule. 63 engines have now been delivered. I would like to acknowledge the commitment demonstrated by the team here in its production. HAL is also enhancing annual production capacity from 30 to 50 engines. These capabilities directly contribute to the sustained operational readiness of the IAF’s Su-30MKI fleet.”On increasing helicopter engine capacity, Rajnath said, “India’s growing fleet of indigenous helicopters requires a strong and reliable indigenous engine ecosystem. HAL is establishing a second production line for Shakti engines at Koraput, adding to the existing capability at Engine Division, Bengaluru. Together, these facilities will strengthen our capacity to support platforms such as the ALH and LCH and meet the evolving requirements of the armed forces. A stronger engine ecosystem is essential to a stronger self-reliant defence capability.”

articles.title: Robert Redford bought 2 acres in Utah for his family in 1961; he later bought a canyon and turned it into Sundance, an arts and conservation retreat
articles.summary: Robert Redford, the actor and director who died in September 2025 at the age of 89, bought two acres in Utah's Provo Canyon in 1961 as a place for his
articles.body: Robert Redford, the actor and director who died in September 2025 at the age of 89, bought two acres in Utah's Provo Canyon in 1961 as a place for his family. Over the following decades, he assembled the surrounding land into Sundance Mountain Resort, which became home to the Sundance Institute, the Sundance Film Festival, and preserved wilderness areas. Redford wanted to develop the canyon without damaging it, so he kept buildings small, rustic, and blending into the landscape. Today, the resort stands as an arts, film, and conservation destination shaped by one man's devotion to the land.How the Provo Canyon land passed from its Ute inhabitants to the Stewart familyArchitectural Digest's 1989 home tour, written by Judith Thurman with photography by Dick Busher, republished in 2025, begins with the canyon's past. In 1900, the federal government sold the glacial bowl at the foot of Mount Timpanogos to the Stewart family, a Mormon family. They bought 3,500 acres at two and a half dollars per acre, pastured sheep there, and eventually built a small ski station with one lift and a Samoan-style restaurant. Before settlement, the magazine notes, the canyon was a Native American hunting and fishing ground. The resort's own story names the Ute as its original inhabitants.What led to the two-acre purchase in 1961 and why Redford fell for itRedford loved this semi-wilderness long before he owned any of it. Travelling home to Los Angeles from college in Colorado, he passed through the canyon and kept returning to camp there. He later studied painting in Florence and moved to New York to act on Broadway, but his marriage to Provo-born Lola Van Wagenen cemented his tie to Utah. In 1961, the couple bought their first, very modest piece of local land, two acres. The magazine describes the view as an upturned palm of alpine meadows and glacial rock. The resort adds that a ride up the canyon in 1961 left him spellbound.How Redford built a family house in 1963, then bought a canyon in the late 1960sRedford summed up his early approach to Architectural Digest with a joke, do another television show, buy another acre. In 1963 he built a small family house on the land, doing the construction himself, which he called the first important thing he had accomplished. By the late 1960s, after several hugely popular films including Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid, he had the means for a bigger gamble. He told his lawyer, "I want to buy a canyon," the magazine reports. The purchase forestalled a rumoured plan to divide the land into quarter-acre lots. The resort says he owned thousands of acres by 1968.For the next ten years, Sundance was a low-key, stylishly rustic ski resort with some of the finest powder in the West. Redford recalled a mess behind the charm, he could not get a bank loan, vehicles stalled, waiters did not turn up, sewers backed up, the resort was robbed, and the tree in the Tree Room restaurant died. He was wary of promotion and fiercely protective of the canyon's privacy. He bought out original partners who could not understand why he refused to expand. His lesson was that keeping something intact means keeping your own vision of it intact.How Redford's idea of development shaped rustic buildings that blend into the landRedford came to see Sundance as a small-scale version of the larger challenge facing planners and environmentalists. He asked how one can develop without causing development. His answer came from his own craft, develop the place the way a photograph is developed, by bringing its details into focus without violating the frame. He wanted a place big on ideas and small on buildings, with a rustic shell designed to disappear into the landscape. Limestone, tree-trunk columns, and rough-hewn local cedar echoed the canyon's geology, while facilities stayed modern. The resort's story condenses this into "developed a little, preserved a lot."Redford told Architectural Digest that running a resort was never his ambition. In 1979 he attended an independent film festival in Salt Lake City and realised that experiments were happening in remote places and going unseen. He concluded that Sundance could host a community of artists, with the ski business supporting the arts rather than the reverse. The institute, established in the early 1980s, first offered summer fellowships to screenwriters and directors chosen for original feature scripts. Fellows spent a month in a film laboratory led by mentors including Sydney Pollack, Waldo Salt, and George Roy Hill. Redford said artists there get permission to fail, with no production rules.How Redford's Institute for Resource Management and decades of activism brought environmental causesRedford founded the Institute for Resource Management in 1982, a nonprofit forum at Sundance meant to humanise the debate between the energy industry and environmentalists. Negotiations it sponsored led in 1986 to a pact on offshore drilling in the Bering Sea. The magazine's 2025 introduction adds that he served as a trustee of the Natural Resources Defense Council for 30 years and was elected commissioner of the Provo Canyon sewer district in the 1970s. Disillusioned with politics, he turned to independent activism and filmmaking, including the Redford Center for environmental films. He received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016.How 50 developed acres, 450 recreation acres, and preserved wildlife habitat balanced Sundance's land use50 acres were under development, holding the rehearsal hall, screening room, gift shop, two restaurants, private homes, and rental cottages. Another 450 acres were devoted to skiing and recreation, and an area was set aside to restore wild game. Grouse, mule deer, elk, groundhogs, and a few moose were flourishing again, alongside six rare species of hawk and eagle. Artists were encouraged to come up for mountain solitude. Today the resort says about 70 per cent of its land is permanently preserved, with 4,000 acres set aside for nature conservation.For 20 years, Redford collected Native American art and artefacts, amassing more than 600 pieces that spilt from his home into public spaces. In the Tree Room, a large Navajo weaving from about 1930 covers the back wall. Curator Brent Beck, Vice President of the Sundance Group, says Redford began with Navajo rugs while making Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid, to the puzzlement of his financial advisers. The collection spans ancient pottery, historic weavings and beadwork, and modern works. Beck recalls an ancient bowl sitting beside Redford's Oscar for Ordinary People. Redford said he enjoys such ironic pairings because the art reminds him that everything is sacred and nothing is.Redford's own house is a plant-filled solar home from the 1970s, built of wood, glass, and fieldstone, whose finest feature is its setting. It includes a windowless music room shaped like a Pueblo kiva, a small round office in a stone tower, and a thinking room above it with no telephone. Redford called the house an environment for his collection, not a museum. The hillside cottages, designed by Salt Lake City architect John Shirley, keep a low visual impact, and Redford dried wildflowers from his rides to decorate them. An Indian blessing, as the magazine calls it, opens each summer session of the institute.How Sundance changed hands in 2020 and what the resort offers todayRedford sold the resort in 2020, when it spanned 2,800 acres, and he died on 16 September 2025 at home at Sundance, the place he loved. Today the resort says its lodging, lifts, art studios, galleries, restaurants, and spa sit within preserved land. It lists six dining establishments, one Michelin Key designation, twelve artists in residence each year, and an Inn with 63 mountainside rooms. Classes at the Art Studio and Gallery, concerts, skiing, hiking, mountain biking, and fly fishing continue the mix of creativity and outdoor play that Redford imagined.You use AI every day. 'WE NEED TO RETURN IMMEDIATELY,' FLIGHT CREW WARNS AS PILOT HEALTH EMERGENCY UNFOLDS Air Canada flight AC785 had just arrived to Los Angeles from Toronto when it was being towed to the gate, the airline told Fox News Digital. articles.title: ED unearths bribe racket involving top executives of 40 PSUs, banks & companies
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Enforcement Directorate has unearthed a bribery racket involving top executives of at least 40 public sector undertakings and government banks,
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Enforcement Directorate has unearthed a bribery racket involving top executives of at least 40 public sector undertakings and government banks, besides some corporate houses engaged in siphoning off and laundering hundreds of crores of corporate social responsibility (CSR) funds channelled through multiple charities promoted by a class XII dropout, who has been caught impersonating as a medical doctor for close to three decades.According to ED, the fake doctor, Dharmendra Kumar Chandradev, received CSR donations in his multiple trusts registered for the purpose of laundering money meant for charity and exempted from taxation. These funds were further returned back to the "donor" in cash, after retaining his commission. The racket involved some corporate houses, hospitals, public sector companies and govt banks. Top executives of these PSUs were heavily bribed for releasing CSR funds.On Oct 1, the central agency carried out searches at eight locations across Maharashtra, Bengal, Gujarat and Delhi-NCR related to these bogus donations cases. The agency seized several pieces of evidence and details of transactions related to PSU executives and corporate hospitals, in addition to Rs 21 lakh in unaccounted cash."The CSR mechanism was utilised as a conduit for conversion of accounted funds into unaccounted cash. Funds amounting to Rs 200 crore have been routed through the above mechanism," ED has estimated through its preliminary investigation.The agency further said its probe revealed that CSR contributions from corporate houses were "returned substantially in cash" to the contributors after deduction of a small commission.Searches have also revealed a network of agents and intermediaries who channelled CSR funds to the trusts, which were thereafter routed through shell entities controlled by market operators. Most of these entities have also been flagged in multiple GST fraud investigations."At least 40 PSUs and public sector banks across the country have provided CSR donations to the trusts operated by the accused. Several projects were only partially executed or not executed in proportion to the funds received, while vendor bills were inflated and excess funds routed through bogus or shell entities. Kickbacks and commissions were allegedly paid to intermediaries facilitating the CSR funding," ED said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Punjab government moves Supreme Court against CBI probe into 'bribe syndicate' linked to CM Bhagwant Mann's OSD
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Hours before CBI carried out searches at Punjab CM Bhagwant Mann's camp office in Chandigarh and registered an FIR against his OSD and others,
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Hours before CBI carried out searches at Punjab CM Bhagwant Mann's camp office in Chandigarh and registered an FIR against his OSD and others, Punjab govt had rushed Supreme Court to urgently hear its appeal against Punjab and Haryana HC's Monday order directing the agency to probe ED's allegation that a bribe syndicate influenced transfers, postings, tenders and policy decisions through an OSD in the CM's office.Fearing imminent coercive action - based on the HC order for registration of an FIR - by CBI against top politicians and bureaucrats in the state, the Mann-led AAP govt in its appeal sought an urgent stay of the HC's directions. "If the impugned judgement is not stayed, CBI will register an FIR against high public functionaries of the state on untested material... and the situation will become irreversible," it said.Senior advocate Vikas Singh, appearing for the state govt, said HC had brushed aside the state's preliminary objections, declined three weeks to Punjab Police to complete the preliminary inquiry, which it initiated based on ED's communication levelling "cash-for-transfers postings" allegation, and directed a CBI probe, contrary to the federal scheme of governance mandated by the Constitution."Please hear the petition today itself at 2pm," Singh requested a bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana. When the bench said it was impossible to take the appeal for hearing Tuesday itself, Singh said the appeal must be heard Wednesday, suggesting the development can have potentially a huge political fallout in the poll-bound state and arguing that the order marked a breach of the federal scheme of governance.The bench said the state's petition will be listed for hearing either Wednesday or Thursday.In its appeal, the state govt revealed ED's Jalandhar zonal office on July 30 sent a 150-page communication to Punjab DGP under PMLA, alleging it was found that one Nihal Gohal, whose premises were searched in May, influenced transfers, postings, tenders and policy decisions "through an officer on special duty in the office of CM".DGP marked the communication, large parts of which were illegible, to Punjab Bureau of Investigation on Aug 3. The bureau began its preliminary inquiry within two days and started collecting evidence from different departments. It sent reminders to ED on Aug 28, Sept 2 and Sept 5, asking it to depute an officer with complete records, but no cooperation was received till Sept 7, the state claimed.HC had ordered a CBI probe because of what it held to be inaction in the registeration of an FIR on the material evidence sent by ED and had said, "Prima facie allegations with regard to scams including cash for transfers, cash for getting favourable policies, cash for tenders, and such other illegal activities corruption in high public offices have been substantiated by ED with reference to various WhatsApp chats and other information..."Punjab govt said the high court erred by sending CBI into a state which had withdrawn consent to the agency needed to carry out an investigation in the state's jurisdiction, without citing any exceptional circumstances that warranted a CBI probe.In 2010, SC had ruled that SC and HCs can direct a CBI probe in exceptional cases even in states which have withdrawn general consent.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.summary: Kick streamer TokyoHarri went viral after an associate was punched during an IRL livestream in Shibuya, Tokyo.
articles.body: Kick streamer TokyoHarri went viral after an associate was punched during an IRL livestream in Shibuya, Tokyo. The incident happened on October 4, 2026, during a now-deleted stream. A tourist approached the streamer’s associate from behind and appeared to hit him in the face before leaving through the crowd. TokyoHarri then appeared to chase after him. Online posts later accused the streamer and his associate of using offensive language toward the tourists before the punch. Those claims have not been independently confirmed. No police charges or official findings related to the incident have been reported.TokyoHarri associate punched during Shibuya livestreamTokyoHarri, also known as Tokyo Interviews, is a Japan-based creator known for street interviews, nightlife content and interactions with people in Tokyo.The October 4 livestream showed TokyoHarri and his associate in Shibuya when a tourist suddenly approached the associate from behind. The man threw a punch that appeared to land on the associate’s cheek. The associate then moved out of the camera’s view while the tourist walked away. TokyoHarri could be seen following him.The video was later deleted, but a clip from the stream continued to circulate on X. Industry reporter @doxpopolie described the people involved as TokyoHarri and his “sidekick” and claimed they had been “trolling” tourists before the confrontation.That account also accused the pair of using racial slurs and offensive words. Those claims came from the social media post and were not confirmed by police or another official source.Some Reddit users who said they watched part of the deleted VOD gave a similar account. One user, u/Qberi, claimed the associate had used a racial slur and made comments about the tourist’s acne before the confrontation became physical.Another user, u/c0mb00, criticized the streamer’s associate over the alleged comments.However, those comments are from viewers and should not be treated as an official account of what happened. The deleted VOD also means the full exchange is not currently available for independent review.TokyoHarri faces fresh attention after previous Japan incidentThe latest incident has also brought attention to an earlier confrontation involving TokyoHarri in Japan.In October 2025, footage from one of his IRL streams showed a man objecting to being filmed in the Shinjuku area. The man appeared to tell Harri not to point the camera at him before pushing the camera away.The footage later showed another confrontation involving a woman after Harri’s drink was kicked. Reports about the incident have differed, and there has been no reliable public confirmation establishing the full circumstances or whether police took action against the streamer.That distinction matters with the latest Shibuya incident as well. The available clip shows the punch, but it does not show everything that happened before it. Claims about what was said before the attack remain allegations from social media users.As of October 6, no charges or official findings connected to the Shibuya confrontation have been reported. TokyoHarri has also not been publicly confirmed as facing any criminal case over the incident.For now, the clearest part of the story is what the video appears to show: TokyoHarri’s associate was punched during the livestream, the tourist left the scene, and TokyoHarri followed him. articles.title: In 2021, Georgia police aircraft destroyed $37,000 worth of legal hemp; six years later, Supreme Court revives grower’s claim, overturning 60-year-old precedent
articles.summary: The Georgia Supreme Court has revived a legal battle over whether the government must compensate property owners when law enforcement operations damage
articles.body: The Georgia Supreme Court has revived a legal battle over whether the government must compensate property owners when law enforcement operations damage their property, ruling that the state cannot automatically avoid the Georgia Constitution’s just-compensation requirement simply by invoking its “police power.”According to a report by Reason published October 4, the unanimous ruling involves Blue 42 Organics, LLC, a licensed hemp grower whose crops were allegedly destroyed during a Georgia Department of Public Safety (DPS) drug-suppression operation in 2021.Police aircraft allegedly destroyed $37,000 worth of hempAccording to the Georgia Supreme Court’s opinion, Blue 42 operates a hemp farm in Dahlonega and was properly registered with both the Georgia Department of Agriculture and the U.S. Department of Agriculture.On July 21, 2021, DPS, acting through the Governor’s Drug Suppression Task Force, conducted a drug-suppression operation in the area. Three helicopters and a single-engine fixed-wing aircraft allegedly flew at such a low altitude over Blue 42’s farm that two rows of legally registered hemp crops were destroyed.The company valued the damaged crops at approximately $37,000. Blue 42 also alleged that the low-flying aircraft harassed cattle on leased grazing land, potentially jeopardizing future lease renewals.Blue 42 subsequently sued DPS, asserting an inverse-condemnation claim under the Georgia Constitution’s Just Compensation Clause. The provision states that private property cannot be “taken or damaged for public purposes” without just and adequate compensation being paid.However, a trial court dismissed the company’s claim after accepting DPS’s argument that the damage occurred while the agency was exercising its police powers. The Georgia Court of Appeals later upheld that decision, effectively preventing Blue 42 from pursuing compensation.Supreme Court rejects blanket police-power exemptionThe Georgia Supreme Court disagreed with the lower courts.Writing for the unanimous court, Chief Justice Peterson said the state’s police power is extremely broad, covering government actions intended to protect public health, safety, morality and welfare. But the court concluded that this power cannot create a blanket exemption from the constitutional obligation to compensate owners whose private property is damaged for a public purpose.The court wrote that the Constitution’s protection of private property rights would be rendered “an empty one” if the state could avoid paying compensation simply by invoking its police power.The justices specifically rejected the reasoning of McCoy v. Sanders, a 1966 Georgia case that had been used to support the idea that property damage resulting from an exercise of police power did not require compensation.In McCoy, police had drained a landowner’s pond while searching for the body of a murder victim. The government was not required to compensate the owner for the resulting damage because the action was considered an exercise of police power.Nearly six decades later, the Georgia Supreme Court concluded that the broad rule established by McCoy went too far. The court formally overruled the relevant portion of that precedent.Court preserves narrow exceptionsThe ruling does not mean that every instance of government property damage during police or emergency operations will automatically require compensation.The court identified two established categories in which the government may remain exempt: abatement of nuisances and destruction of property in cases of urgent necessity.The justices cited the example of a government destroying a building to prevent a fire from spreading. Such emergency action can fall within the narrow exception to the compensation requirement.But the court found that Blue 42’s allegations did not establish either exception at the motion-to-dismiss stage. The justices therefore reversed the lower court’s decision and remanded the case for further proceedings.That means Blue 42 has not yet won a $37,000 judgment. Instead, the company has regained the opportunity to pursue its claim for compensation in court.Ruling could affect broader property-rights disputesThe Georgia case comes amid a wider legal debate over whether innocent property owners should receive compensation when police damage or destroy their property while pursuing suspects.Similar disputes have involved homeowners and businesses in other states. Reason has previously reported on cases involving Indiana homeowner Amy Hadley, California business owner Carlos Pena and Texas homeowner Vicki Baker, whose properties were damaged during law-enforcement operations involving other people.The issue has also reached the U.S. Supreme Court. In 2024, Justice Sonia Sotomayor, joined by Justice Neil Gorsuch, said in connection with Baker’s case that the question of whether a police-power exception exists under the Takings Clause was “an important and complex question” that would benefit from further development in lower courts before the Supreme Court intervened.Baker later prevailed under the Texas Constitution, according to Reason, adding another state-level development to the broader debate over government responsibility for property damaged during law-enforcement operations.You use AI every day. articles.title: Ukrainian drone attack sets fire to oil tanker carrying 23 Indians off Russia's Black Sea coast; crew rescued
articles.summary: A Ukrainian drone attack set fire to a Liberian-flagged oil tanker carrying 23 Indian crew members off Russia’s Black Sea coast on Tuesday, with all those
articles.body: A Ukrainian drone attack set fire to a Liberian-flagged oil tanker carrying 23 Indian crew members off Russia’s Black Sea coast on Tuesday, with all those aboard later rescued, Russian authorities said.Russia’s transport ministry said the tanker, Aframax Rio, was attacked by “naval drones” on Tuesday, triggering a fire in the Black Sea near the Russian resort city of Sochi.The ministry said there were no injuries among the crew, according to Reuters.The ministry said emergency crews rescued all 23 people aboard the tanker.The attack caused crude oil to burn openly in the Black Sea, according to the Russian transport ministry.🔥🚢A massive fire is burning near the Russian Black Sea port of Sochi in Krasnodar Krai after an oil tanker was hit. Special Kherson Cat 🐈🇺🇦 (@bayraktar_1love) October 6, 2026Firefighters were initially unable to tackle the blaze because of its intensity, but the ministry said they had sufficient means to fight the fire once it became less intense.Indian crew rescued as tanker catches fireThe vessel was carrying a crew made up entirely of Indian nationals.The tanker was reported to be on fire off Russia’s southern Krasnodar region, with a large cloud of black smoke visible from Sochi. Authorities in the Sirius federal territory closed beaches following the incident, while water and air quality were being monitored.“According to atmospheric air quality monitoring data, pollutant concentrations in the Sirius Federal Territory remain many times lower than the maximum permissible concentrations and pose no threat to health,” Dmitry Plishkin, head of the Sirius federal territory administration, said.The Russian transport ministry said the tanker was attacked by an unmanned vessel.Attack comes amid wider Black Sea shipping risksThe incident took place amid a series of attacks involving commercial shipping in the Black Sea since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.Both Russia and Ukraine have heavily targeted commercial shipping around the Black Sea during the conflict. Russia has in recent days attacked grain vessels carrying Ukrainian goods near the coast of Romania.Earlier on Tuesday, a Russian strike on a merchant vessel flying the Marshall Islands flag in the Black Sea killed at least one crew member and injured several others.The vessel was carrying rapeseed oil and caught fire after its superstructure was damaged.Two other merchant ships, the Togo-flagged Alfa Watan and Palau-flagged Able, were also hit by drones of unknown origin about 112 kilometres off Bulgaria’s coast.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy denied that Ukrainian forces were behind those strikes near Bulgaria.Sochi coast placed under restrictionsVideos and photographs circulated on social media showed large flames burning offshore and a thick column of black smoke over Sochi.Sochi Mayor said access to the coast and beaches was being restricted. Beaches in Sirius were also closed following the tanker fire.The Aframax Rio was reportedly near the Russian coast when the attack took place. Russian independent media had reported the incident, while MarineTraffic had last located the tanker in the Black Sea near the Russia-Georgia border.The vessel was included on Ukraine’s sanctions list as part of Russia’s so-called “shadow fleet”, according to The Kyiv Independent.India raises concern over attacks on shippingThe tanker incident comes amid attacks on commercial vessels in other key maritime routes involving Indian crew members.The ministry of external affairs had earlier condemned an attack on MV Royad Mammadov in the Black Sea, in which two foreign seafarers were killed and some crew members, including three Indian nationals, were injured. The three Indians were reported safe after receiving medical treatment in Romania.The MEA also condemned an attack on the Panama-flagged MT On Peace off Oman while it was transiting the Strait of Hormuz. The vessel had 19 crew members, including 17 Indians, and 12 crew members were injured, including 11 Indians, according to the ministry.The MEA said India viewed attacks on commercial shipping and seafarers with “grave concern” and called for dialogue and diplomacy to end ongoing conflicts.In September, India and Liberia also launched a 25-nation “Group of Friends on Safety and Security of Shipping and Seafarers” at the UN General Assembly to work towards the safety and security of merchant crews and commercial shipping against targeted attacks, according to the MEA.You use AI every day. articles.title: U.S. resident charged with helping Canadian school shooter in rampage that killed 8
articles.summary: Jesse Van Rootselaar, 18, killed her mother and stepbrother and then five students and a teacher at a secondary school in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia, in February.
articles.body: A 30-year-old Washington state resident was charged with providing assistance to a teenager who killed eight people in Canada, including schoolchildren, U.S. prosecutors said Tuesday. James Cody Bryant, who the FBI said identifies as female, was arrested Tuesday and is charged with conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country in connection with the Feb. 10 shootings in the British Columbia town of Tumbler Ridge, officials said. Prosecutors said Bryant had been in contact over Discord with the shooter, who killed five children and a teacher at a secondary school, as well as two other people. He gave the shooter advice and money and offered to help livestream the killings, the U.S. Justice Department said. Bryant “had been in repeated contact” with the shooter, the acting U.S. attorney for the Western District of Washington, Neil Floyd, said at a news conference Tuesday. Bryant “had the information and ability to alert law enforcement, and even discussed that possibility with the shooter — but chose not to,” Floyd said. “Instead, he encouraged and offered assistance to a murderer.” About 2 p.m. Feb. 10, Jesse Van Rootselaar, 18, who was born male but had been transitioning to female for six years, killed her mother and 11-year-old stepbrother in the small town of Tumbler Ridge, officials said. She then went to Tumbler Ridge Secondary School and killed five children — three 12-year-old girls and two boys, one 12 and the other 13 — and a teacher, authorities said. Van Rootselaar then died by suicide. The rampage was one of the deadliest shootings in Canada’s history. In addition to those who were killed, two other children were shot and seriously wounded, officials said. Bryant tried to talk Van Rootselaar out of the attack or get her to reconsider several times but did not tell law enforcement about the plan and offered to livestream it, the U.S. Justice Department said. The two met on the former random video chat service Omegle around three years before the shooting and kept in contact through Discord, an online communication service, said W. Mike Herrington, special agent in charge of the FBI’s Seattle office. There is no indication the two ever met in person, he said. The back-and-forth messages on Discord cited in the complaint have a conversational and friendly tone. At one point, Bryant writes, “You believe me when I promise I won’t snitch on you, right?” At another point, Bryant tells Van Rootselaar, “if you are uncertain, maybe take it as a sign.” On the day of the shootings, after Van Rootselaar killed her mother and stepbrother, she had trouble starting her car, Floyd said. “Bryant provided advice and offered assistance on how to get the car started so that JVR could proceed to the school and kill children,” Floyd said, using the initials for the shooter’s name. The charge of conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country carries up to life in prison. Bryant was in custody Tuesday, officials said. Online federal court records did not show an attorney representing Bryant on Tuesday afternoon. The shooting was livestreamed on Twitch, but for only about 20 seconds before it shut off, officials said. Twitch said an account appearing to be Bryant’s was the only account that saw it, according to the criminal complaint. Herrington, of the FBI, said the shooter wanted maximum views but didn’t have much of a social media presence. “Without Bryant’s misplaced loyalty and willingness to operate the livestream, we don’t ultimately know if the shooter would have gone through with the crime,” Herrington said. “We certainly know that the shooter was concerned that not enough people would see the livestream.” Elija Rain, assistant commissioner of the British Columbia Royal Canadian Mounted Police, said the impact of the shooting was widespread. “The people of Tumbler Ridge experienced a tragedy that forever changed the lives of families, friends, students, educators, first responders and the entire community,” he said.

articles.title: Christa Pike is conscious and speaking as she recovers from failed execution, her lawyers say in new update on her condition
articles.summary: "She's still in the hospital on a ventilator, critically ill," attorney Stephen Ferrell said. "We don't really know the prognosis yet and may not know for se...
articles.body:
Christa Pike is conscious and speaking in the hospital after surviving Tennessee's attempt to execute her last week, her lawyers said Tuesday.

"Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care. Despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed. Her recovery is medically unprecedented. Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery," her legal team wrote in a statement released to the media.

Pike had been unconscious and in critical condition in the days after two doses of pentobarbital failed to end her life on Wednesday, Sept. 30, according to her attorneys.

Dr. Joel Zivot, a medical expert who has consulted with Pike's legal team, told the Associated Press that the latest update "bodes well for a good recovery," but said that the full picture of her long-term health won't be clear for some time.

"She has recovered to a certain degree that she's able to be off a ventilator and able to speak, but in no way would I announce her free of further serious risk," he said. "There's still a lot of bad things that can happen here."

Fallout from the failed execution has brought intense scrutiny to Tennessee's execution procedures. Gov. Bill Lee suspended the one remaining execution scheduled for this year and announced that the state's top prison official would be stepping down.

In a statement, Correction Commissioner Frank Strada said resigning was "in the best interest of Tennesseans" while an independent review examines what happened on Sept. 30.

Strada will leave at the end of October, and an interim commissioner will be named later, Lee said.

Pike's lawyers said the resignation "is justified, but it does nothing to help Christa now."

"What happened to her Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person," they said in a statement, according to ABC News.

"I think at the very least the governor should commute Ms. Pike's death sentence to a life sentence," attorney Stephen Ferrell said on CNN's State of the Union on Sunday. "We don't know what her physical state will be, but it is clear that she has endured a torturous attempt at executing her."

Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of her classmate, Colleen Slemmer. Her execution was scheduled to be carried out after 30 years on death row. But the execution was called off after the drugs she was administered did not kill her. She was taken to the hospital, where she received life-saving care.

Both of Pike's arms were "swollen, burned, and blistered" when she arrived at the hospital, her lawyers wrote in a legal filing. Her lawyers believe the IV lines were placed incorrectly or her veins burst, so that some or all of the drug went into the tissue of her arms instead of her bloodstream.

The filing asks a state court to order the Tennessee Department of Correction to preserve all evidence from the execution attempt.

"Last night was not just inefficient, it was cruel, and it was torturous," attorney Randy Spivey said the day after the execution attempt. "It was also predictable."

Spivey said Pike's legal team warned the state of Tennessee and the courts that her medical condition of thrombocytosis "would cause her to suffer an agonizing death." They said it could increase clotting and pain during the execution process and that her veins are difficult to access. Pike's attorneys said the state and the court dismissed their client's concerns.

In audio recordings obtained by the New York Times , Pike had said two weeks before she was due to be executed that she was concerned about the lethal injection, citing a recent botched execution attempt in Tennessee of Tony Carruthers in May, when staff were unable to locate a vein. "Tony Carruthers lived out my worst nightmare," Pike can be heard saying in the audio, which was shared by her lawyers.

"I do not have good veins,' she said. "And I don't want to go through that."

"She was not seeking to delay her execution," attorney Stephen Ferrell told reporters on Oct. 1. "She was seeking to have that execution performed humanely and as quickly and as painlessly as possible."

Following the failed execution, Lee ordered "a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred" and said that another execution scheduled for Dec. 3 later this year had been paused.

"This is a tragedy," he said. "There is no one who wanted what happened last night to happen. It's deeply disturbing to me that this has happened in this state."

Pike's attorneys said in response that the governor's independent review doesn't go far enough after being in solitary confinement for more than 20 years and the botched execution attempt. "Christa has endured punishment greater than any other person in the history of the American death penalty," Spivey said. "The governor must commute Christa's sentence now.

May Martinez, the mother of Pike's victim, Colleen Slemmer, told NBC News the execution attempt had been a "mess," adding, "They didn't say anything, and then, all of a sudden, they asked all the victims to leave. We didn't know anything until we got up to the office and saw the commissioner. And he said that it didn't work ... and she's on her way to the hospital."

U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the state's Republican candidate for governor, said Tennessee should look at other forms of execution. "If it's lethal injection, if it is electric chair, what we do know is we have to find a way to do this — and do it successfully," she told The Associated Press.

Tennessee officials have not said whether they will try to execute Pike again, or explained what went wrong.

Her condition could complicate any future attempt. Under Supreme Court precedent, a person can't be executed unless they have a "rational understanding" of why they are being put to death, the New York Times reported . Dr. Joel Zivot, an Emory University anesthesiologist retained by Pike's defense team, told the BBC it is "very possible" she suffered a brain injury because resuscitation was delayed.

Pike's lawyers have asked Lee to commute her sentence to life in prison. Lee had denied her clemency before the execution attempt.

President Trump questioned how the execution could have failed, telling reporters it "shouldn't be very difficult," according to AFP . United Nations human rights chief Volker Türk urged Tennessee not to try again.

What happened during the execution attempt?

Pike had been scheduled for execution at 10 a.m. Wednesday for killing Slemmer in 1995, at the age of 18. She would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.

An appeals court stopped the lethal injection just an hour before it was to start, a stay that was subsequently overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court.

Media witnesses said officials raised the curtains to the execution chamber at 7:27 p.m., showing Pike strapped to a gurney. "I'm going to leave this world the way I spent most of my life, and that is in love," she said in her "last" words.

However, Pike remained conscious after the first dose. Nashville Banner reporter Steven Hale said she lifted her head off the gurney at 7:54 p.m. She also reportedly asked prison officials if her arm was supposed to feel that way.

Tori Gessner, a journalist with WKRN News 2 in Nashville, said Pike was seen pointing at her arm and asking, "Does this happen like that?"

By 8:26 p.m., witnesses reported that the second dose of pentobarbital had been administered.

Pike continued to be heard snoring behind the closed curtain until the microphone was cut off at 8:53 p.m. At that time, an announcement was made to escort media witnesses out of the area.

Pike's legal team said in a statement to the Tennessean newspaper on Wednesday night, "We take no pleasure in being right, but the concerns raised by Ms Pike proved to be true: difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy."

Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said what Pike experienced was "singular and unparalleled."

Seven other people have survived medical problems caused by an execution team's failure to access a vein to administer lethal injection drugs, but no one has remained alive after receiving the drugs used in such executions, she said.

"I've witnessed, I believe, five executions in Tennessee," Gessner said. "Nothing about today was normal, typical at all, and the court delay was just the tip of the iceberg."

A source told NBC News that there was no medical oxygen or mask in the execution chamber, meaning they had to be brought in from a prison clinic. Some of the medication had worn off by the third time staff checked on Pike, the source added.

The Tennessee Department of Correction said that it "followed every step of the state's lawful, established execution protocol approved by the attorney general's office."

The state's execution protocol calls for a secondary set of drug syringes to be administered "if the inmate is not deceased" after the first set. It does not specify what happens if the subject is still alive after the second set.

Lawyers for Pike filed an emergency motion late Wednesday with the Tennessee Supreme Court seeking to immediately halt and stay the execution, saying she was in "unnecessary agony" and that the execution was violating her right to be free from cruel and unusual punishment. They also filed motions in the Sixth Circuit and a district court.

Pike was sentenced to death in 1996 after being convicted of first-degree murder of Colleen Slemmer the previous year on the University of Tennessee Agricultural campus.

According to legal documents filed with the Supreme Court , Pike "tortured, and killed Colleen Slemmer" on Jan. 12, 1995 because Pike "just felt mean that day." Pike is reported to have cut Colleen's throat multiple times and crushed her skull with a piece of asphalt.

Pike was also convicted of attempted first-degree murder after trying to strangle fellow inmate Patricia Jones in 2001.

Strada took over Tennessee's Department of Correction in January 2023 after serving as deputy director of Arizona's prison system. In late 2024, he announced Tennessee would switch to a single execution drug, pentobarbital.

Death penalty lawyers told the Guardian that Pike's was the fifth "botched" execution Strada had overseen in two states since 2022. That count includes Tennessee's failed attempt to execute Tony Carruthers in May, when staff couldn't find a vein, and three 2022 executions in Arizona in which teams struggled to place IV lines.

Kit Thomas, a death row attorney, told the Guardian that training requirements for execution teams were loosened under Strada. "He reduced the training requirements and we've seen disastrous results," Thomas said.

A day before announcing the resignation, Lee defended the department, telling reporters, "So far as we know, the Department of Correction followed exactly the protocol that was outlined."

According to the Death Penalty Information Center (DPIC), there were 75 botched lethal injections between 1982 and 2010. Compared to other methods, lethal injections face complications at a significantly higher rate. There have been a number of botched executions since 2010 that don't appear in the DPIC's tally.

Most of these were executions that went wrong in some way, but still ended in death. But there are seven known instances in which an execution failed entirely. One of them was earlier this year in Tennessee, when staff were unable to find a vein to administer the lethal drugs to inmate Tony Carruthers.

More than 20 pharmaceutical companies have also refused to have their products used in executions, which has left states struggling to find the drugs they need to perform lethal injections. In some cases, they have experimented with unproven alternatives, with disastrous results.

An Oklahoma prisoner named Michael Lee Wilson said he could feel his "whole body burning" as he was being executed using a controversial drug cocktail in 2014. There have also been instances of prisoners gasping for air , heaving and coughing , convulsing and being subjected to "three hours of pain" before finally dying.

In April 2022, Tennessee called off the execution of Oscar Smith about an hour before it was scheduled to begin after the state discovered that its lethal injection drugs had not been properly tested. An independent investigation found that the state had repeatedly failed to follow its own drug-testing protocols between 2018 and 2022.

Tennessee then revised its protocol, resuming executions in May 2025 and using a single, lethal drug: pentobarbital.

There's also growing evidence that lethal injection may not provide a peaceful death even when everything appears to go right.

Difficulties with lethal injections have led some states to revive previously discarded execution methods. South Carolina carried out three executions by firing squad last year. There had been three total firing squad executions in the U.S. in the previous half-century combined.

There were 47 executions in 2025 , according to the DPIC, higher than the recent average of fewer than 30 per year. These included the lethal injection of South Carolina inmate Marion Bowman , who received twice the intended drug dose, and Tennessee inmate Byron Black , who reportedly showed sustained cardiac activity for nearly two minutes after prison staff pronounced him dead.

articles.title: From Gujarat CM to India's PM: Modi's 25 years in office
articles.summary: Narendra Modi was thrust into the thick of governance in 2001 as the party suffered a setback in local polls in Gujarat and the response of the state
articles.body: Narendra Modi was thrust into the thick of governance in 2001 as the party suffered a setback in local polls in Gujarat and the response of the state government headed by CM Keshubhai Patel to the massive Kutch earthquake was found wanting.Within months of his swearing-in as CM, riots swept the state in the wake of the Godhra train-burning incident. BJP's win in the 2002 assembly polls cemented his position and dissidents in the party were marginalised as he set about implementing his governance agenda.Oct 2001-May 2014: Gujarat CMKutch rebuilt. In 2003, Gujarat passed India's first state disaster management law.Vibrant Gujarat Summit launched in 2003 to showcase its strength & attract investors.Jyotigram Yojana, launched in 2006, prioritised reliable power supply over subsidised but erratic electricity to villages. Soon, all 18,000 villages had access to reliable three-phase power as non-farm economic activity expanded and subsidies were nearly halved.Sagarkhedu Sarvangi Vikas Yojana launched in 2007 adopted an outcome-oriented mission for coastal communities, combining infrastructure, livelihoods, irrigation, salinity control, coastal security and fisheries development.Launched in 2009, Garib Kalyan Mela took welfare delivery to citizens.Check dams, farm ponds, recharge wells, canals and inter-basin transfers were planned as surplus floodwater was carried through 332km of canals and Narmada water reached reservoirs across Saurashtra, opening over 10 lakh acres of irrigation potential. A CAG report in 2017 recorded groundwater recharge roughly 50% above 2002 levels.His government linked ports with power, roads, rail and industrial estates. Mundra, Hazira and Pipavav grew into major private ports.Nudged by RSS, the BJP brass named Modi in June 2013 as its campaign committee head for the 2014 polls and soon elevated him as its PM candidate. When results were announced on May 16, BJP more than doubled its tally to 282, its first majority in the then 545-member Lok Sabha. It was the first majority government since 1984.2014-2019: First term as PMHis government launched Jan Dhan Yojana, and 59 crore accounts were opened with over Rs 3.1 lakh crore in deposits. Women owned 33 crore of these accounts. This helped in ushering in direct benefit transfer, changing welfare delivery. By Aug 2026, DBT had transferred Rs 53.2 lakh crore across 320 schemes and 56 ministries.In his Aug 15 speech at Red Fort, Modi spoke of the indignities women suffer due to lack of toilets and announced a sanitation campaign. Swachh Bharat Mission was launched. PM Ujjwala Yojana, launched in 2016, gave 10.5 crore free LPG connections to women from poor households by May 2026.His government expanded the social security net, including free treatment for the poor under Ayushman Bharat. By 2025, official estimates say 94.3 crore Indians were covered by some form of social protection, up from 19% in 2015 to 64%.GST was rolled out in July 2017 in what the PM lauded as economic unification of India as tax borders came down and the market became one.2019-24: Second term as PMFew people outside the top echelons of government were aware when it took probably its most significant political calls: revoking the special constitutional status enjoyed by J&K under Article 370, downgrading the state to the status of UT and hiving off Ladakh as a UT.A verdict from SC paved the way for construction of Ram Mandir in Ayodhya. The idol was consecrated in Jan 2024.CAA was passed in 2019, providing a path to citizenship for persecuted non-Muslim communities from Pakistan, Bangladesh and Afghanistan.The Covid pandemic and lockdowns tested government as India suffered a large human toll. Scaling up of indigenous vaccines and the world's largest vaccination campaign helped. Government launched the Atmanirbhar Bharat programme. It was also a period when UPI use began zooming and has become a definitive success.2024: Wins a third termBJP went into the 2024 elections with supreme confidence and was humbled as a section of voters balked at its "abki baar 400 paar" slogan. However, it won a majority with its allies even as it lost its own majority after a decade.A manufacturing push in semiconductors, startups and self-reliance continues to be the focus. Govt cited India's high growth rate to emphasise handling of global headwinds.Security forces' success in virtually eliminating Naxalism, cited by predecessor Manmohan Singh as the biggest internal threat to India, has been a boost to BJP's national security agenda.Operation Sindoor targeted terrorist hideouts in Pakistan in May 2025 after the Pahalgam attack.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 3 of Nolan Wells’ friends sue NFL Hall of Famer Terrell Owens alleging defamation
articles.summary: The suit alleges Owens defamed them by posting on X: “ARREST THEM IMMEDIATELY!!” The post also linked to a video that theorized the three killed Wells, according to the lawsuit.
articles.body: JACKSON, Miss. — Three friends of Nolan Wells, a Black college student who went missing from a Mississippi island during a Fourth of July celebration and was later found dead, are suing NFL Hall of Famer Terrell Owens alleging defamation. Lawyers for the friends said they intend to file several more defamation claims this week against content creators and have previously indicated their intent to sue the Rev. Al Sharpton and “The View” co-host Sunny Hostin for comments they made while discussing Wells’ death. The fathers of the three friends, who are under 21 and considered minors under Mississippi law, filed the federal lawsuit Monday on their behalf. The lawsuit alleges Owens defamed the three friends after posting on X: “ARREST THEM IMMEDIATELY!!” Owens’ post also linked to an Instagram video, which theorized the three friends killed Wells and tampered with his phone, according to the lawsuit. The post was made days after a Mississippi grand jury declined to recommend charges in Wells’ death. Owens has 1.2 million followers on X and had previously pledged $25,000 to a reward fund for information leading to an arrest and conviction in Wells’ death. “Not only is he defaming them, he’s basically saying to the mob, get your pitchforks, get your torches,” said Edward Paltzik, a defamation and media attorney representing the three friends. The Associated Press attempted to contact Owens through social media and SMAC Entertainment, which, according to its website, manages Owens, but did not immediately receive a response. The three were part of a group of 30 friends, including Wells, who rode to Horn Island on three boats on the Fourth of July. Wells’ friends said Wells did not return to the mainland with them, choosing instead to stay behind to talk with a girl, a claim his family has disputed. His body was found two days later off the island’s coast. Neirher state nor independent autopsies have determined Wells’ cause of death, though the grand jury found his death was “consistent with drowning.” Wells’ family and their lawyers disputed the grand jury’s findings, pointing to unexplained bruising on the back of his head and noting that his airways and stomach were devoid of water. Images showing Wells with white friends the day he went missing fueled online speculation that racial dynamics played a role in his death. Two of the three friends who are suing Owens were singled out online in part because they appear in a photo with Wells and one other friend on a boat, which was circulated on social media after his disappearance. The third called Wells’ mother and the Coast Guard to report Wells missing.

articles.title: Christa Pike lawyers say she is speaking one week after failed execution
articles.summary: The 50-year-old has regained consciousness and is receiving care nearly one week after being sent to the hospital.
articles.body:
Lawyers for Christa Pike say she is awake and able to speak after her botched execution attempt by the state of Tennessee on September 30.

Tuesday’s statement marks the first public indication that Pike’s condition has improved after she was transported to a Nashville hospital after receiving two doses of pentobarbitol, lethal injections intended to end her life.

Her failed execution has sparked debate about the use of the death penalty in the United States. Pike is thought to be the first person to have survived such an injection in the country.

“Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care,” Pike’s lawyers said in a statement.

“Despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed. Her recovery is medically unprecedented. Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery.”

The statement also expresses gratitude to medical workers who the lawyers say have “treated Christa like a human and have provided exceptional care to her”.

Pike’s lawyers had previously stated that she was unconscious and on a ventilator. They described her arms as “swollen, burned and blistered” by the failed execution.

Pike was convicted and sentenced to die in 1996 for her participation in the murder of a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, when she was 18 years old. Two co-defendants received lesser sentences.

Pike’s defence lawyers had pointed to her mental health struggles in their attempts to commute her sentence. But the Slemmer family had advocated for the death penalty, pointing to the violent nature of the 19-year-old’s murder.

Accounts of Pike’s failed execution describe her kicking off the sheet covering her body and, at one point, appearing to snore. She reportedly expressed feeling pain as the lethal injections were administered.

The incident has brought attention to the prevalence of botched executions in the US criminal justice system.

Critics have argued that botched executions — defined as those that deviate from established procedures through unforeseen issues, delays or administrative incompetence — can cause unnecessary pain and suffering for those being put to death.

Citing the researcher Austin Sarat, the Death Penalty Information Center, a nonprofit, estimates that 3 percent of executions in the US from 1890 to 2010 were botched.

articles.title: UK risks being 'uninvestable' if new oil and gas fields not approved, warns Equinor
articles.summary: Equinor warns it may shun further investments in the UK if new oil and gas fields at Rosebank and Jackdaw are not approved.
articles.body:
Oil giant Equinor has warned it may shun further investments in the UK if new oil and gas fields at Rosebank and Jackdaw are not approved.

"The question will be: is the UK investable in the future? I hope it will not come to that," said Anders Opedal, boss of the Norwegian state oil company which is part owner of the sites.

He told the BBC the company would "have to take a hard view about it" if a decision was made to reject new drilling.

The warning comes as the UK government is set to decide whether or not to grant final approval to extract oil and gas at Rosebank and Jackdaw, despite a ban pledged in Labour's election manifesto.

The government said any decision would take into account all relevant evidence.

Rising energy prices have prompted renewed debate over the UK's energy security, with UK production forecast to halve by 2035.

The UK already relies on Norway for half of its gas needs, and the Norwegian government has continued to issue new licences for oil and gas exploration in its own North Sea waters.

Equinor has predicted production will remain at current levels until the middle of the next decade.

Opedal said he remained confident that Prime Minister Andy Burnham's talk of a "pragmatic approach to oil and gas" meant both projects would get approved but he said the current limbo was "an uncomfortable position to be in".

He said that the UK could produce more of its own oil and gas.

"It's a political choice," he said. "The North Sea oil and gas industry started on the UK side. We learned from the UK and it's actually the same geology on both sides of the border - several fields actually cross it."

Rosebank is the United Kingdom's largest undeveloped oil and gas field, located in the North Atlantic about 80 miles north-west of the Shetland Islands and is thought to hold up to 500 million barrels of oil and gas.

Opedal told the BBC the exploration licence for the site was originally granted 25 years ago. "The licence was awarded in 2001, the discovery was made in 2004 and the final investment decision in 2023," he said.

Both Rosebank and Jackdaw were initially given the go-ahead by the former Conservative government but were delayed by a legal ruling from a Scottish court, after environmental groups argued consent was given without fully considering the climate impact.

Following a public consultation on the sites, which closed in August, the final decision now rests with Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh.

Both Jackdaw and Rosebank are operated by Adura, a joint venture between Equinor and Shell. Aberdeen-based firm Ithaca also owns 20% of Rosebank.

Adura has previously said that if approval comes soon, Jackdaw could start delivering gas to UK homes by this winter as the construction is "99% complete".

Tessa Khan, executive director of Uplift, an organisation that wants the UK to move away from fossil fuel production, said new drilling at Rosebank "won't cut our bills" and was a "bad deal for Britain".

"It's overwhelmingly oil for export – but it will make Equinor and its part-owner, the Norwegian government, richer, while Britain is left with high energy bills and a declining workforce."

Khan said Labour's "climate credibility is also on the line".

A government spokesperson said the North Sea remained a "vital national asset", adding that "oil and gas will continue to play an important role in our energy system for decades to come - alongside transitioning to clean power to protect jobs and tackle the climate crisis".

"Any decision will take into account all relevant evidence, including environmental assessments and public representations received during the consultation process," the spokesperson added.

articles.title: Order of the Sinking Star: Jonathan Blow on making ' the biggest puzzle game ever'
articles.summary: Order of the Sinking Star is due out on Thursday and has roughly 1,500 puzzles for players to try
articles.body:
For ten years, Jonathan Blow has been working with a small team on what he believes is "the biggest puzzle game ever made".

The American developer is renowned as one of the fathers of the modern indie game movement, creating the genre-defining puzzle-platformer Braid in 2008.

Now, a decade on from his last project, The Witness, The Order of the Sinking Star is due to be released on Thursday - a game with roughly 1,500 puzzles that he estimates could take around 500 hours to complete.

So why make something the majority of players may never get even halfway through, let alone finish?

"Some people decide what to make based on what's practical or what makes business sense," Blow says. "It's never been the way that I think."

"I sort of make bad business decisions in a sense...because I let the design dominate that process. But then because we did that, we always have something unique," he says.

The game's blurb likens itself to a "game design supercollider" - four worlds viewed from overhead, built on the mechanics of four pre-existing free puzzle games from other designers (with their permission to do so).

These ideas are then "smashed together" to create brand-new brainteasers.

For example, one world's mechanics, based on those from the free 2014 game Mirror Isles by Alan Hazelden, sees players use mirror reflections to swap places across islands.

When combined with the system of another free game created by Hazelden, Skipping Stones to Lonely Homes - where players throw stones into water to create paths - brand-new puzzle opportunities suddenly arise.

How an AI was tricked into breaking its own rules

Taking a risk on making something more experimental is what appears to ultimately drive Blow, who says that as the industry has grown, the culture for developers has also changed.

"Somewhere along the way...this idea that the best designers were trying to always make new experiences...just sort of got dropped by the wayside," he says.

The outspoken designer is renowned for his frank takes on the industry - previously calling social media games such as Farmville "evil" and World of Warcraft's quest design "unethical".

In December 2025, Hazelden publicly distanced himself from Blow - writing in a post on Bluesky that he was "dismissive of diversity efforts" and "pro-MAGA".

Blow, who has not responded to these critiques publicly, tells me he instead decided to "sit down and focus on the games".

"What the players want from developers is good games," he says.

"They don't want us to be arguing, especially with each other, about political stances."

Blow says he is sceptical of AI, which was "not part of the pipeline at all" for Order of the Sinking Star, even though he recognises it as an "advancement" and an "interesting technology".

Of the benefits often cited by those who use the tech, such as increased productivity, he asks: "If you're saying you're ten times as productive and it's been 3 years, you should have been able to do thirty years of work."

"So where's this output of 30 years of work?"

Despite rejecting the tech, Blow says the industry faces an "uncertain time" in how it deals with AI, particularly with newer creators who may rely too heavily on it to code rather than learning the "weird glyphs" themselves.

"A danger is that not many people know how to program in the future," he says.

"And if AI can't really do everything, then the supply of programmers might not be enough to make good stuff."

Blow's refusal to compromise on any aspect of the Order of the Sinking Star transcends its core design.

The developer decided to make his own programming language, Jai, from scratch.

He then used this, alongside a custom engine, to make the game.

A game's engine is a piece of software that packs everything needed to craft a playable experience - including graphics rendering, physics simulation and scripting - into one place for creators.

Some developers turn to pre-built game engines such as Unity or Unreal Engine, rather than taking on the considerable challenge of building an engine from scratch.

For Blow, creating his own engine in this language meant he could build something "tuned and authored very specifically" to what he wanted to make.

It is yet another reason he gives for why this project, which started as a simple "design experiment", has taken ten years to finish.

"I do want the next project after this to be less on hard mode, or really it was nightmare mode, because we did so many things on hard mode at the same time," he reflects.

"But it's also been rewarding in a certain way. Because otherwise, what else are you in the industry for?"

articles.title: Froyo's made a comeback. But at £12 a tub will it last?
articles.summary: Frozen yoghurt, which was a huge craze in the 2000s and 2010s, has made its return with multiple chains popping up across the wider UK.
articles.body:
Kiersten Paterno was one of the many people willing to queue up to an hour to treat herself to some frozen yoghurt.

"It was a 45-minute wait for my turn but the whole experience of choosing your flavours and customising it with different toppings was a big part of the appeal for me," the 19-year-old student says.

Froyo was a huge trend in the UK in the late 2000s and early 2010s and was most popular in London.

Chains like Snog had 10 stores in the capital at its peak and other brands like AngelBerry had shops in Bristol and Brighton.

And this year it's made a comeback, driven by nostalgia, social media and its perception as a healthier dessert choice.

Several brands such as Go Greek, Myka and Yo-Chi launched in London, while Frurt, which operates mainly in the north west of England and Yorkshire, has opened new stores, including one in Leicester.

These companies saw hundreds of customers queueing to create their own dessert pot, despite it not being a particularly cheap treat, with tubs costing as much as £12.

Kiersten says she was initially attracted to the dessert as she could manage portion size and sweetness level.

"I could control how sweet I wanted it to be through the toppings. It feels healthier overall as it's a dessert I can enjoy without feeling like I've overindulged."

She admits it can be pricey but says she doesn't mind spending a little more as an occasional treat.

Research suggests the froyo market is steadily growing. Market Data Forecast estimates that the European frozen yoghurt market is worth £434m in 2026, up from £419m last year.

Australian brand Yo-Chi opened a Notting Hill branch in August and blew up quickly on social media for its range of toppings and "third space" feel.

"Sweet treat culture is huge. People aren't spending a fortune on big things, but a little thing like that, they're happy to," says Bethan Clarke, Yo-Chi campaign manager.

While Yo-Chi would "never call ourselves healthy" - froyo is usually lower in calories and fat than ice cream, but may also contain more added sugar - Clarke says the fact that it is customisable means that people are in control of their own portion sizes and sugar levels.

Social media trends like "2026 is the new 2016" are helping froyo's virality.

"People are coming back to re-experience childhood a little bit," says Clarke.

Ella Light, who also works for Yo-Chi, says she's been surprised by the mix of people coming into the store.

"I was kind of expecting to see the Gen Z girlies coming in, [but] this morning there was a group of builders!"

But how likely is the current froyo craze to survive? After all, it was huge in the 2010s but by the end of that decade was all but dead.

Vhari Russell, founder of Food Marketing Experts, says: "Market over-saturation played a role in the initial disappearance of froyo, as well as the natural cycle of dying trends."

Market leader Snog faced increasing competition from the likes of Yog, Yoomoo and Pinkberry, while consumers also realised that the dessert may not have been the healthier option they initially thought it was.

"But now 2010s throwbacks coupled with a modern twist are seeing huge appetite across the market," says Russell.

Will £12 for a tub eventually start to put people off though?

Russell doesn't believe so, as she calls it an "affordable luxury".

Going out for a froyo can be "an experiential moment" as much as anything, she adds.

"For many people, they don't smoke or have expensive lifestyles, so froyo isn't viewed as food, it's viewed as an experience."

Not interested in queuing for two hours? Here's how to make your own

If the price of froyo seems unreasonable or if you can’t justify queueing for hours, BBC Food have five different froyo variations you can make at home.
