articles.title: Coyotes choose the front of a couple's Southern California cabin for an early morning scrap
articles.summary: Surveillance footage captured three coyotes brawling for 40 minutes outside a Southern California cabin in the San Bernardino Mountains area.
articles.body: The mystery surrounding why a couple's dog barks in the middle of the night at their Southern California cabin has been solved thanks to some early morning surveillance footage. The footage revealed three coyotes right outside David and Annette Simpson's front door of their cabin in the San Bernardino Mountains. These wild animals weren't there to ask to borrow any sugar either. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS They were there to fight. And fight they did for about 40 minutes, starting at around 1 a.m. Sunday morning. The couple wasn't at home during the scrap in front of their cabin, but the action was caught on their surveillance cameras. What do you do with forty minutes of a coyote fight? Well, naturally, you don't want it to go to waste, so you post it on social media, then sit down for an interview with the local news. "We wonder why our dog barks in the middle of the night, and now we know," Annette Simpson told KTLA. TWO MASSIVE ALASKAN BROWN BEARS FIGHT OVER PRIME FISHING SPOT AT LAKE CLARK NATIONAL PARK Indeed. It must be due to those rambunctious coyotes. While nature doesn’t come calling at your door every day, a dog will certainly know when it does. They've seen bears, squirrels and other wildlife before, but not a coyote scrap on the walkway in front of the cabin. That's a new one for these two. Are they worried about how close the coyotes were to their cabin? Not Annette. She's into it. OUTKICK IS NOW ON THE FOX APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD "I think it’s pretty cool. We really enjoy watching the wildlife and just so close," she said. "Those stairs just lead right to our front door, and they came up those stairs." They enjoy watching it, but they don’t want it messing with their own domesticated animals. Annette, who said she sometimes lets her cats out on the patio, is reconsidering after watching the footage of these coyotes.

articles.title: 80% vote in West Bengal bypolls amid rigging, intimidation charges
articles.summary: KOLKATA/CHENNAI/GUWAHATI: Bypolls across three states and one Union territory saw high but uneven turnouts Tuesday, with Bengal's Nandigram and Rejinagar
articles.body: KOLKATA/CHENNAI/GUWAHATI: Bypolls across three states and one Union territory saw high but uneven turnouts Tuesday, with Bengal's Nandigram and Rejinagar recording 80% turnout amid allegations of rigging, voter intimidation and police interference, while polling in one Puducherry and two Tamil Nadu assembly seats and Assam's Nagaon Lok Sabha constituency remained largely peaceful.Nandigram recorded above 80% turnout by 7pm, but voters reported being turned away from booths. CM Suvendu Adhikari, who had vacated the seat after winning both Nandigram and Bhowanipore in May, said: "In 2016, I won by 82,000 votes, my highest margin ever. I believe that record will be broken this time."Congress candidate Milan Pradhan, out on bail following his arrest in a 2007 case after he filed his nomination, said the election had been "looted" and complained of blocked agents, voters being denied entry, assault and vandalism. CPI and ISF candidate Sabe Mirza Khan also alleged rigging.Rejinagar recorded 80% turnout, with allegations of police interference dominating polling. AJUP chief Humayun Kabir, who gave up Rejinagar and kept Nowda after winning both in May, was detained after police accused him of provoking tension. Videos showed police grabbing Kabir by his shirt and taking him away. He was released after 12 hours. His son Golam Nabi Azad is the AJUP candidate.Congress and TMC alleged widespread rigging and removal of polling agents. BJP's Shankharavh Sarkar clashed with central forces after being asked to move away from voters.Tamil Nadu saw a turnout dip from April's elections. Madurantakam recorded 86%, down from 93%, while Dharapuram saw 80%, against 89% in April. Both saw three-way contests involving TVK, DMK and AIADMK.Assam's Nagaon Lok Sabha bypolls recorded 76% turnout. BJP's Devasish Sharma, Congress's Sibamoni Bora and AIUDF chief Badruddin Ajmal are the main contenders among 15 candidates.Puducherry's Thattanchavady recorded 78% turnout by 5pm, with final figures expected to rise. articles.title: Meet the Monarchs: The ‘endangered’ 3,000-mile traveller butterflies that survive on poisonous milkweed diet
articles.summary: Picture this: Every autumn, one of nature’s most extraordinary journeys begins with a creature weighing less than even a gram!
articles.body: Picture this: Every autumn, one of nature’s most extraordinary journeys begins with a creature weighing less than even a gram! Millions of monarch butterflies, light as a feather, take to the skies across North America, travelling thousands of miles from their summer breeding grounds towards overwintering forests in Mexico. Some eastern monarchs can even travel up to 3,000 miles (about 4,800 km) during the migration. Quite an astonishing distance for an insect whose wings can fit comfortably across the palm of a hand!Then again, Monarch butterflies are famous for this epic migration, but lately, their story is tinged with real concern. In 2022, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) declared the migratory monarch butterfly Endangered. Habitat loss, pesticides, climate change, and ruined wintering forests have slashed their numbers. Those in the west have been hit especially hard. At the heart of their world sits milkweed, which is a plant that’s toxic to most creatures, but critical for monarchs.Why do monarch butterflies need milkweed?For monarchs, milkweed isn’t just food; it’s the only option. Female monarchs lay eggs exclusively on milkweed. Caterpillars hatch, then chomp down on nothing but milkweed leaves. The plant is loaded with cardiac glycosides, which are basically chemical toxins. For most animals, these compounds spell trouble.But monarch caterpillars have evolved immunity. They eat the leaves and store some of the poisonous molecules in their bodies. When a caterpillar matures into a butterfly, that toxicity remains, offering a shield against predators. The monarch’s bold orange-and-black coloring acts as a warning: “Eat me, and you’ll regret it.” Predators learn fast and usually steer clear.So, what poisons most animals serves as a nursery, a food source, and a chemical defense for monarchs.How can a butterfly travel 3,000 miles?This is something amazing and almost unbelievable about the butterflies: the monarch migration isn’t completed by a single butterfly!The eastern population heads south from Canada and the US, aiming for the central forests of Mexico. The trip is long: sometimes over 3,000 miles. Monarchs can cover 70–75 miles in a day, depending on the weather.The spring migration north breaks up into generations. Butterflies arriving in Mexico reproduce, die, then the next generation flies north, repeating the process. So, each butterfly does just a stretch of the journey.Then, in autumn, you get the “super generation.” This batch lives for up to eight months—much longer than the usual four-week lifespan. These butterflies hold off on breeding, stock up on energy, and make the whole journey south. Monarchs seem to time their travel using cues like day length and temperature.Why are monarchs at risk?It’s not just fewer butterflies that are at risk of extinction; whole landscapes that monarchs rely on are disappearing.The IUCN ties their decline to the loss of milkweed, habitat destruction, pesticides, and climate shifts. Farms and herbicides wipe out milkweed, so there's no place to lay eggs or feed caterpillars. Logging in Mexico’s overwintering forests, plus California’s, wrecks the butterflies’ refuge.As for climate change, it complicates everything. Drought stunts milkweed, extreme weather knocks out butterflies, migration gets out of sync, and food sources aren’t ready.The numbers on the western population are jaw-dropping. From the 1980s to 2021, they dropped roughly 99.9%: from millions down to barely 2,000 in the winter count.Are monarchs officially protected?It’s complicated. The IUCN marks the migratory monarch as Endangered, but the US hasn’t finalized federal protections. As of September 2026, they’re still being considered for listing as “threatened” under the Endangered Species Act. The main threats, like habitat loss, climate change, and insecticides, are clear, but official action is still in the works.However, one doesn’t have to wait for a law to help. Preserving wild habitat, growing native milkweed, keeping nectar-rich flowers available, and cutting out unnecessary pesticides make a big difference.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. articles.title: Jaguar launches new electric car after 'woke' ridicule
articles.summary: Two years after JLR relaunched Jaguar into a blizzard of controversy, it has unveiled its new electric car.
articles.body:
Two years ago, Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) relaunched Jaguar into a blizzard of controversy. Its bizarre teaser ad was described as "woke" and its "Barbie pink" concept car was ridiculed.

Now, the first of its new models has appeared in public for the first time. The all-electric Type 01, unveiled in New York, represents a radical new direction for the classic brand.

The car itself is an imposing four-door "Grand Tourer", with a long bonnet that deliberately harks back to Jaguar's emblematic 1960s E-Type.

But it marks a gamble for JLR, which has invested billions reinventing Jaguar and is facing mixed reactions over the new car's design and the brand's all-electric strategy.

The new model's electric motors are potent, producing about 1000 horsepower and allowing it to accelerate from 0-62mph in 3.2 seconds. JLR says it has a range, at "sustained highway speed", of up to 320 miles.

The company describes it as the "most technically advanced, powerful and aerodynamic Jaguar ever engineered".

However, it comes at a hefty price tag, with a minimum cost of £130,000 ($172,426). In the US, the Type 01 has a starting price of $130,500.

Under normal circumstances, the launch of a car like this might generate few headlines. But in this case the attention has been much greater, and for good reason.

In 2024 Jaguar unveiled its new identity to the public. The first step was a surreal advert, showing models in a range of bizarre and brightly coloured outfits. There was a new Jaguar logo - but no cars in sight .

Two weeks later, Jaguar's denim-clad design chief Gerry McGovern took to a Miami stage to unveil a pair of radical concept cars, resplendent in Miami Pink and London Blue colour schemes. "Jaguar has no desire to be loved by everybody," he quipped.

The event was meant to herald Jaguar's future as a luxury all-electric marque, but it triggered a furious backlash in the press and on social media.

Critics claimed JLR was betraying its heritage in favour of going "woke". Even the colour chosen for the launch was derided as "Barbie pink", as culture wars erupted around it.

The reception appeared to catch JLR by surprise. The reinvention of Jaguar as a luxury electric brand was part of a wide-ranging strategy set out by the company in early 2023, in which it pledged to invest £15bn in new models and technologies.

At the time, Jaguar itself was struggling. The badge, which was once an intrinsic part of Swinging Sixties British cool, had lost its lustre. Where in the past it had supplied E-Types to Brigitte Bardot and Steve McQueen, it now struggled to sell upmarket saloons and SUVs to middle-ranking corporate executives, who generally preferred Audis and BMWs.

"Jaguar's core demographic, despite the uproar, gave up on the brand years ago, so they effectively had nothing to lose," explains Matthias Schmidt of Schmidt Automotive Research.

The unveiling of the Type 01 was met with mixed reactions, with some on social media criticising the new car.

"Looks like a Cybertruck and a Bentley Continental had an illegitimate child," Facebook user Ken Katch said, referring to the Tesla pick-up, known for its polarising design.

Craig Kinnersley, who runs a luxury car consultancy, wrote on LinkedIn that it is an "unmitigated catasthrophe" that looks like a hearse and lacks any "memorable Jaguar flourish".

"We are watching the people running JLR dance on the brand's grave." he added.

Car content editor Keith Adams said he was torn over the car's looks but that the companty deserves credit for "producing something genuinely distinctive rather than another anonymous premium EV".

"At least it isn't boring," said another Facebook post.

JLR wound down production of its old Jaguar models in 2024 and 2025. The "woke" row, while it possibly made life briefly uncomfortable for the company's leadership, did at least keep the Jaguar name in the public consciousness at a time when it was selling very few cars.

"It brought Jaguar from the back pages to the front pages, given that it was dying in a crowded international market," says Schmidt. "Everyone is now talking about what would have been another boring product."

The GT is expected to be the first of three new electric designs from Jaguar.

Since that event in Miami two years ago, McGovern has left the company, JLR has parted ways with the agency behind the controversial rebranding campaign, and the company also has a new chief executive.

But the future of Jaguar itself still hangs in the balance.

"I think it really is a last throw of the dice," says automotive journalist Steve Fowler. "JLR has struggled to make serious money with Jaguar in the past, and that's what it's all about."

The question now is whether enough buyers can be found willing to pay £130,000 for a relatively distinctive upmarket electric car, in a market where they can also choose models from the likes of Porsche, Mercedes-AMG or even fast-growing Chinese brands such as Denza.

"Forget the controversy, the culture wars and the pink concept car," says Ginny Buckley of the electric car website Electrifying.com.

"What ultimately matters is whether Jaguar has built something extraordinary enough to justify blowing up everything it stood for before."

She believes the car is good enough to silence critics, but admits "the next challenge will be getting people to buy it".

Steve Fowler agrees. "The car is good enough to do it," he says. "Whether the Jaguar brand is good enough remains to be seen."

articles.title: Former CIA officer pleads guilty to stealing nearly $200M in gold bar case
articles.summary: The $200 million in payments dwarfs previous amounts disclosed in the case.
articles.body:
The former CIA officer arrested after authorities discovered roughly $40 million worth of gold bars in his Virginia home pleaded guilty in federal court on Tuesday to a single count of wire fraud, admitting he defrauded the U.S. government out of nearly $200 million for his personal benefit.

David Rush was previously described by prosecutors as a "master manipulator" who used his clandestine position to amass millions worth of gold bars and luxury watches -. though the government revealed in Tuesday's hearing the extent of his alleged deception far exceeded what was previously known to the public.

The nearly $200 million in payments to Rush, which dwarfs previous amounts disclosed as part of his case, will likely only further draw public and congressional scrutiny to the intelligence community to provide more transparency regarding its methods in doling out taxpayer dollars to agents and the oversight that follows such exchanges.

The case has drawn widespread intrigue and raised major questions regarding the intelligence community's management in overseeing the secretive systems that grant officials like Rush the ability to amass high-value assets tied to their work.

According to a summary of his plea agreement provided by a senior DOJ prosecutor, Rush is alleged to have engaged in two separate criminal schemes where he fabricated so-called Special Access Programs to convince senior officials to clear payments to him totaling over $190 million that he sought to use for his personal benefit.

In the first instance, prosecutors said Rush received approximately $145 million that he used to purchase luxury real estate properties in Palm Beach, Florida, and then carry out home improvements so he could then flip them and sell for a profit. Portions of the $145 million also went toward purchases of luxury vehicles and watches, all while Rush is alleged to have lied to officials that he had clearance for the payments from high-level officials in the Trump administration.

A second scheme, prosecutors said, involved Rush's fabrication of a separate program that resulted in officials approving 298 gold bars to be provided to him that he later falsely claimed had been distributed, until the roughly $46.4 million worth of gold was discovered in a search of his residence in May.

Rush also admitted to fraudulently seeking compensation for roughly $1.8 million in charter flights that were for his personal benefit.

Another previously unreported disclosure from Tuesday's proceedings included an admission by Rush that he once disclosed top secret information to a foreign government official regarding the identity of a U.S. clandestine source. Prosecutors did not identify the foreign government who received the information or Rush's motives in sharing the source's identity, however.

"Following an internal investigation that identified potential crimes, CIA immediately referred this matter to the FBI," said CIA Director John Ratcliffe. "David Rush abused his position and betrayed the public trust and should be held fully accountable for his actions. We appreciate our law enforcement partners in the FBI and Department of Justice for securing this outcome. The Agency is committed to ensuring that those entrusted with our Nation's secrets are held to the absolute highest standard."

Attorney General Todd Blanche said, "Federal employees are entrusted with serving the American people, not themselves. The Trump Administration is committed to rooting out waste, fraud, and abuse in the federal government, including by prosecuting those who foolishly defraud American taxpayers."

Rush has remained in government custody since his arrest in May, despite only facing initial charges of theft of public money that accused him lying about his background and committing time card fraud regarding claims about military leave.

The single wire fraud charge Rush pleaded guilty to Tuesday carries a maximum potential sentence of 20 years in prison and Rush separately agreed to $195 million in restitution as part of his plea.

Rush's sentencing has been set for Jan. 28 of next year.

articles.title: Facing stonewalling from Russia, Trump admin struggles to plan for potential plague fallout
articles.summary: The Trump administration is struggling to get clear answers about the death of a Russian laboratory worker at an institute dedicated to studying the plague,...
articles.body:
The Trump administration is struggling to get clear answers about the death of a Russian laboratory worker at an institute dedicated to studying the plague, amid days of stonewalling from Russian officials about the mysterious circumstances surrounding the episode.

The death of the technician at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia immediately raised alarms throughout the administration, prompting a race to compile intel and plot for a potential public health response, according to multiple sources familiar with the matter.

But Russia's reluctance to share information about the incident has complicated those efforts, leaving officials uncertain what broader risks it could pose — and how exactly to defend the US against them.

The US is considering issuing a formal diplomatic communication, called a démarche, to Russia for more information, a source familiar told CNN.

"It's incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday . "Maybe it's bigger than we thought. We don't know, but I think it would be reckless at this moment, given the limited information we still have, to speculate."

US officials were in touch with the Russian government as early as last Friday, a State Department official said, including contact between the department's health experts and the Russian Foreign Ministry. And that outreach has continued, an administration official said, as Rubio expressed hope Tuesday that the limited information sharing "will change in the next few hours and days."

President Donald Trump told reporters outside the White House Tuesday afternoon that he had "call scheduled" to speak with Russian leader Vladimir Putin about the issue "very soon." He added US agencies would have more information to report "probably tomorrow."

But the US has gotten limited cooperation so far. What little information has come out of Russia has faced deep skepticism, with officials unconvinced that the Kremlin is being fully forthcoming, according to people familiar with the situation.

Still, until the administration knows more through intelligence collection and diplomatic outreach, officials are not taking steps such as putting travel restrictions into place to prevent any potential spread, according to a US official. The US already advises against travel to Russia due to various factors, including the possibility of wrongful detention and the war with Ukraine.

Among the critical questions still outstanding: whether the 28-year-old lab worker who died last week contracted pneumonic plague — a severe but treatable infection — or another, unknown infectious disease. Staff at the Anti-Plague Institute study a range of other dangerous diseases, including cholera, anthrax and brucellosis, according to the institute's website .

US officials have also sought details on whether the disease was modified in any way, a process called gain of function that could dramatically alter the way the US and other countries might respond.

Rubio and other Trump officials have publicly downplayed the immediate threat to Americans, emphasizing that the administration is closely monitoring the situation and that pneumonic plague is treatable with antibiotics.

But behind the scenes, there is deep unease within the administration over the continued lack of insight, the people familiar with the situation said. Compounding those concerns is the Russian government's outsized response, including quarantining the hospital where the lab worker was treated, according to the mayor of the Shelekhovsky district. Nearly 200 people are under observation , a regional news outlet reported.

"We don't know a lot right now about what actually happened," said one US official. "But one thing most of us feel certain about: The Russians are going to act like the Chinese did with Covid. They won't be forthcoming."

Still, Trump on Monday characterized the situation as a "big problem" for Russia, suggesting that the US might need to provide some unspecified level of aid.

In a statement, a State Department spokesperson said that several federal agencies were "closely monitoring the fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague," but that many of the details surrounding it remained unconfirmed. They reiterated that Americans have long been advised not to travel to Russia for any reason.

"We encourage Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and openly," the spokesperson said.

In the days since the lab worker's death, the National Security Council and State Department officials have led the administration's push to gather information, piece together what happened and evaluate the potential risks, officials and others familiar with the situation said. Federal health agencies, including the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response, have also been involved in the cross-government effort.

A source familiar with the outreach said Trump officials have also backchanneled with the World Health Organization — the international health body that Trump pulled funding from soon after taking office, but that the government has continued to communicate with in emergency situations.

WHO said Monday that it was in contact with Russian authorities to verify details about the lab worker's death, though it has so far also received little information.

"If they're not transparent, if they're not open to independent accountability, how is it possible to trust the Kremlin is telling us the full and accurate information?" said Lawrence Gostin, a global health law professor at Georgetown University who has worked closely with WHO. "Clearly, on its face, the lab was conducting extremely high-risk research and using shoddy biosafety measures."

The Anti-Plague Institute's relatively remote location in eastern Russia, combined with the pneumonic plague's limited ability to quickly spread, has given health experts some comfort that any immediate threat can be contained.

Pneumonic plague is a bacterial infection , unlike the highly transmissible coronavirus strain that sparked the 2020 pandemic. And while the plague is fatal if untreated, there are now effective and widely available antibiotics to treat it.

While there is little indication that the incident will touch off another global health crisis, officials and outside experts said it has nevertheless reinforced how difficult it can be to monitor and prepare for potential biological threats.

The Health and Human Services Department may have the medical stockpile necessary to combat conventional pneumonic plague, those officials and experts said. But there's little certainty whether it could do the same against a modified version — or how long it would take to develop a treatment if needed.

Jennifer Nuzzo, an epidemiology professor and director of the Pandemic Center at Brown University School of Public Health, said the episode also comes as health response capabilities both in the US and globally have been diminished by funding cuts and the strain of responding to other crises. WHO has proposed slashing its budget following a $600 million shortfall triggered by the US' exit.

America's ability to handle a new public health response, meanwhile, "is severely diminished" amid its efforts to combat measles outbreaks, she said.

"We are talking about a very depleted system. God forbid you layer another pathogen onto the already laborious and difficult work of going after measles," said Nuzzo. "That would be a nightmare."

articles.title: Quote of the day by Pablo Picasso: "There is no abstract art. You must always start with something. Afterward, you can remove all traces of reality"
articles.summary: Pablo Picasso was a Spanish artist who spent most of his adult life in France and became one of the 20th century's most influential painters.
articles.body: Pablo Picasso was a Spanish artist who spent most of his adult life in France and became one of the 20th century's most influential painters. He co-founded Cubism, was a sculptor, printmaker, and ceramicist, and he made an enormous number of works in his lifetime.But beyond just creating art, he also talked about some profound ideas that continue to be relevant even today. He once talked about a quite real-life scenario, about how ideas travel the same road. Every invention, business plan, and story starts as a small seed of something real. Only later does it grow into something others call bold, modern, or even confusing.Let's know what exactly he meant and how it is irrelevant even today.Quote of the dayThere is no abstract art. You must always start with something. Afterward, you can remove all traces of realityWhat does the quote mean?Picasso's line sounds like a riddle at first. How can there be no abstract art when galleries are full of it? Here he doesn’t deny that such paintings exist. Instead, he talks about the origins of where the ideas of these pictures come from.In his view, no artist paints from nothing. There is always a starting point or an inspiration, such as a person, a tree, a memory, or a bowl on a table. Only after that can the artist paint things through his own inspiration, remove things bit by bit, until the result no longer looks like the original. An "abstract" picture, then, is really reality boiled down.His own work shows this. The Cubist paintings he made with Braque in the early 1910s break guitars, bottles, and faces into flat shapes, yet the entire idea and hints keep pulling us back to the real object. Even his other work, Guernica, is also full of distortion and grew out of a real event, the bombing of a Basque town.The origins of these words are usually traced to a conversation between Picasso and the critic Christian Zervos, printed in 1935 in the magazine Cahiers d'Art. It came as a record of words written down by Zervos, not something Picasso wrote himself, and is a translated version of his words.How is the idea relevant even today?Picasso’s idea applies far beyond painting. Digital creativity and the incorporation of arts today begin with basic ideas; for example, app icons and logos. Most are simplified drawings of real things like a handset for "call", a magnifying glass for "search". Designers start with the real object and remove detail until only the idea is left.Similarly, writers also begin with one true moment and let the story grow from it. Startups begin with one real problem before they build a big vision.So, it is just simple that, we don't need to begin with something grand. Begin with something real, look closely, and simplify slowly. The bold, abstract result can come afterwards.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: 'Against all odds': Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike awake and speaking after failed execution
articles.summary: Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike is awake and speaking at a hospital, her lawyers said Tuesday, six days after a failed lethal injection left her
articles.body: Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike is awake and speaking at a hospital, her lawyers said Tuesday, six days after a failed lethal injection left her unconscious and on a ventilator.Pike, 50, survived two doses of pentobarbital during the September 30 execution attempt over the 1995 beating and stabbing death of her classmate Colleen Slemmer.The lethal injection did not kill her, and her lawyers said her arms were left burned and blistered.She was subsequently taken to Vanderbilt University Medical Center for treatment, according to news agency AP.Her attorneys said her prognosis remains unclear and that she faces a long recovery.“Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care,” her lawyers said in a statement. “Despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed. Her recovery is medically unprecedented.”The attorneys also thanked first responders and the hospital medical team for treating Pike and providing care.Doctors say recovery could take monthsPike's latest condition marks the first indication that her health has improved since the failed execution. As recently as Sunday, her attorneys said she remained unconscious and on a ventilator.Dr Joel Zivot, a professor of anaesthesiology and surgery in Atlanta who consulted as an expert for Pike's legal team, said the development “bodes well for a good recovery”.However, Zivot said it could take weeks or months to determine the extent of Pike's recovery and whether her competency could be restored to a level that could allow the state to attempt another execution.“She’s still in the ICU,” he said. “She has recovered to a certain degree that she’s able to be off a ventilator and able to speak, but in no way would I announce her free of further serious risk. There’s still a lot of bad things that can happen here, even when everyone is doing their job well.”A spokesperson for the Tennessee Department of Correction said the department could provide no information other than that Pike remained hospitalised on Tuesday.Lawyers seek records from failed executionPike's attorneys are due in court on Wednesday as they seek information about what happened during the failed lethal injection.They are asking for a court order requiring the Tennessee Department of Correction to preserve evidence from the September 30 execution attempt, including drug lot numbers, records and other information.Chancery Court Judge I’Ashea Myles has scheduled a status conference for Wednesday morning.Pike's lawyers are also continuing to ask outgoing Tennessee Governor Bill Lee to commute her death sentence to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole.“Christa is a survivor and will take recovery one day at a time,” her attorneys said.Lee halted further executions following Pike's hospitalisation and ordered a “comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred”.US Senator Marsha Blackburn, the state's Republican candidate to replace Lee, has called on Tennessee to explore other execution methods to ensure it can continue carrying out capital punishment.Legal questions over another execution attemptPike's survival has raised questions over whether Tennessee could attempt to execute her again, including issues surrounding her competency and constitutional protections.Deborah Denno, a Fordham Law professor who has studied execution methods for 36 years, said Pike has strong arguments that another attempt could constitute cruel and unusual punishment. She also said a second attempt could raise double-jeopardy concerns.In previous cases, states have been allowed to make another execution attempt after failing to establish a suitable intravenous line. Denno said Pike's case is different because she survived after the lethal drug had actually been administered.“They carried out every aspect of the execution,” Denno said. “She didn’t die, but every process they intended, they did it.”Seattle University Law Professor Michael Russo, who has handled capital cases as a public defender in Los Angeles, said the failed execution was horrible but questioned whether the US Supreme Court would prevent Tennessee from trying again on double-jeopardy grounds.“There’s nobody else in the history of the death penalty in this country who has gone through what she’s been through,” Russo said. But he added, “I think what this Supreme Court would say is, her sentence was to die — to be executed — not to suffer an attempt at execution.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Woman allegedly stabs girl after SUV hits semi as soldiers step in to stop horrific roadside attack
articles.summary: Two Joint Base Lewis-McChord soldiers tackled and disarmed a woman who allegedly stabbed a 9-year-old girl after a violent SUV crash on Interstate 5.
articles.body: A woman allegedly stabbed a young girl after sending her SUV careening into a semi-truck and rolling over on a Washington state freeway, prompting two soldiers to tackle her and disarm her. The 35-year-old woman from Steilacoom allegedly threatened two girls with a knife following Monday morning’s crash on southbound Interstate 5 near DuPont, FOX 13 Seattle reported, citing Washington State Patrol. A 9-year-old girl suffered multiple broken bones and a stab wound, while a 15-year-old girl was hospitalized without serious injuries, according to the outlet. WATCH: BYSTANDERS, POLICE LIFT VOLKSWAGEN OFF WOMAN PINNED UNDERNEATH AFTER DRAMATIC E-BIKE CRASH Witness Nathan Wilkinson told KING 5 he was driving to work when he came upon the wreck and saw two men in military uniforms from Joint Base Lewis-McChord intervene. "There's people standing around, then all of a sudden there was a flash, and then the two soldiers jumped on a person. … I heard a scream at that time," Wilkinson told the outlet. "I saw one of the soldiers had a knife in his hand that he had dislodged from the person they tackled." SOUTH CAROLINA WOMAN ACCUSED OF STABBING LYFT DRIVER 11 TIMES CLAIMS MENTAL HEALTH CRISIS Wilkinson called 911 as bystanders subdued the woman, KING 5 reported. FOX 13 reported that two soldiers stopped to help and that photos from the scene appeared to show one holding someone down. CALIFORNIA MOM HAS BOTH LEGS AMPUTATED AFTER SUSPECTED IMPAIRED DRIVER PLOWS INTO HER RESTAURANT LUNCH TABLE Troopers investigating the crash said the SUV struck the left-side barrier, veered toward the right shoulder and then swerved back across the freeway, hitting a semi-truck in the middle lane, according to FOX 13. The SUV struck the barrier again and rolled over. The semi-truck driver was not injured, the outlet reported. FLORIDA MAN ARRESTED FOR DUI AFTER TROOPERS ALLEGEDLY FIND 34 OPEN ALCOHOL CONTAINERS IN VEHICLE Officers told KING 5 that the woman was allegedly driving erratically before the crash. The woman was initially taken to a hospital for evaluation. FOX 13 reported Monday that authorities were investigating her for DUI, vehicular assault and first-degree assault. In a Tuesday morning update, KING 5 reported that she had since been booked into the Pierce County Jail and was expected to face two counts of assault, vehicular assault and two counts of reckless endangerment. Whether those charges had been formally filed was not immediately clear. The cause of the crash remained under investigation, and the woman’s relationship with the girls was not specified in the reports.
